title: A Roman Coin in the Deccan Forest

title_i18n.en: A Roman Coin in the Deccan Forest

subtitle: From Forest Trail to Coin and Crown
era: Pre-Kadamba trade routes and Kadamba economic inheritance, 1st-6th centuries CE
region: Chandravalli near Chitradurga and Banavasi trade zones
moral: Wise rulers build on routes that existed before them.

sources.citation: R. Narasimhachar, Chandravalli excavation report (1909); M.H. Krishna, Mysore Archaeological Department Report (1929); Mortimer Wheeler ASI excavations (1947)
sources.note: Excavation evidence for megalithic and Satavahana-period occupation and foreign coins.

sources.citation: Chandravalli rock inscription of Mayurasharma; cited in Kamath (2001), p. 31 and Ramesh (1984)
sources.note: Kadamba royal presence near the site.

sources.citation: Kadamba copper coins with lion and Kannada legends, including Banavasi Srimanaragi report; Karnataka archaeology reports
sources.note: Evidence for local coinage and Kannada-script legends, with attribution cautions.

panels.shot: dramatic low-angle close on a weathered Roman denarius held in a calloused hand, Deccan forest and distant hill of Chandravalli blurred behind

dialogue.text: In a Deccan forest hollow, a Roman coin, a Han token and a Kadamba name meet, revealing how Banavasi’s rulers inherited an older world of roads, markets and power.

panels.shot: wide bird’s-eye over the bowl-shaped valley of Chandravalli, ringed by low hills and forest, with a shimmering tank at the centre

dialogue.text: Chandravalli, near Chitradurga—today a quiet hollow of trees and rock—was once a crossroads where forest paths, caravans and kings’ ambitions crossed the Deccan sky.

panels.shot: medium shot at ground level of Chandravalli Trader as a generic early 20th-century excavator, kneeling by a trench amid boulders and scrub

dialogue.text: Two thousand years later, men like R. Narasimhachar, M. H. Krishna and Mortimer Wheeler sliced trenches into this earth, reading its layers like pages of a long-buried record.

panels.shot: close-up on Chandravalli Trader’s hands brushing away soil to reveal a silver coin emerging from the dark earth

dialogue.text: From the Satavahana levels came a surprise: tiny disks of distant empires—Roman denarii of Augustus, a Han coin, even a Roman bulla—that had slept in Deccan soil since the first centuries of our era.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of the Roman denarius obverse, faint imperial profile visible against the texture of age and soil grains

dialogue.text: On one coin, the profile of Augustus, first emperor of Rome; on another, the square script of Han China. Little worlds that had travelled by unseen hands to this inland basin.

panels.shot: wide, cinematic view of an imagined Satavahana-era caravan moving through a Deccan forest track, low-angle from the ground

dialogue.text: These coins did not drop from the sky. In the first centuries CE, when Satavahana rulers held the Deccan, caravans threaded forests like these, carrying pepper, textiles and stories along invisible trade veins.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot from behind Chandravalli Trader in the caravan, looking toward a distant Satavahana way-station by a tank

dialogue.text: Chandravalli’s tanks and slopes offered what long-distance traders needed—water, shelter, a watchful eye of local power. Roman and Han coins here mark not tourists, but an older network reaching the Arabian Sea and beyond.

panels.shot: split-level shot showing archaeology trench at top and ghosted image of earlier megalithic stone circles below

dialogue.text: Beneath the Satavahana coins lay older signs—a megalithic world of stone circles and cairns. Chandravalli had been a lived-in landscape long before Rome minted silver or Han officials cast bronze.

panels.shot: medium shot of Chandravalli Trader, now as a Kadamba-period figure, standing before the Chandravalli hill with an inscription rock in the foreground

dialogue.text: Centuries later, another name appears on this landscape—the Kadamba Mayurasharma. His rock inscription near Chandravalli ties his emerging dynasty to this old nodal ground.

panels.shot: extreme close-up of chisel poised on stone, with faint inscription lines already visible

dialogue.text: That inscription is brief, but it is a stake in stone. It says: this forest basin, once a Satavahana stop, now lies within Kadamba reach.

panels.shot: wide, majestic shot of Banavasi townscape in the early Kadamba period, framed by river and fields

dialogue.text: From their capital at Banavasi, the Kadambas did not carve trade from empty rock. They stepped into a world where routes were old, but rulers changed.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of a Kadamba court official handing a palm-leaf grant to a local landholder, with fields visible through an open doorway

dialogue.text: Their innovation lay in how they used this inheritance—issuing agrarian grants, fixing rights over land and water, weaving peasant fields into the arteries that traders had long walked.

panels.shot: close-up of a Kadamba copper coin on a wooden table, lion device clear, with faint Kannada legend around

dialogue.text: Kadamba copper coins carried more than value. Some bore lions and early Kannada legends, quietly proclaiming a local language and symbol in a world used to others’ marks.

panels.shot: medium shot of Chandravalli Trader examining a newly found 'Srimanaragi' coin with scholars around a table strewn with notes

dialogue.text: Recent finds, like a Banavasi coin tentatively read as ‘Srimanaragi’, excite debate. Yet careful voices insist: let evidence, not eagerness, decide what we can truly claim.

panels.shot: wide shot juxtaposing three coins on a dark cloth—Roman denarius, Han coin, Kadamba copper—lit by a single shaft of light

dialogue.text: Laid side by side, the Roman silver, the Han bronze and the Kadamba copper do not tell of Kadambas trading directly with Rome or China. They tell of layered times along the same routes.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Chandravalli forest path today, with Chandravalli Trader walking contemplatively, holding a notebook

dialogue.text: The forest is quieter now. But every shard, every coin, every line of Mayurasharma’s stone reminds us: the Kadambas rose not from emptiness, but from an already humming landscape.

panels.shot: slow push-in close on Chandravalli Trader’s thoughtful face as he looks at the coins in his palm, background fading into abstract maps and routes

dialogue.text: Wise rulers, the Chandravalli story shows, do not boast of creating worlds alone. They read the old routes, respect their depth, and then quietly stamp them with a new, local name.
